author: haiku
reason: Document A explains how the existing system works before proposing anything, puts every limit in one table of fixed values, and keeps the runtime flow (steps 1 to 7, plus a failure summary table) apart from the build and rollout work, while Document B numbers build steps, runtime steps and testing as one sequence and leaves the system facts scattered through its glossary.

author: haiku
reason: B starts by describing the existing system: the page, the rows API, the replica, the queue and the bucket. It then sets out the fixed values, a table of when each column is written, and a summary of failure cases. It also keeps the runtime flow separate from the build and rollout steps, so a newcomer can understand the system faster than from A's single step-by-step sequence.

author: sonnet
reason: A starts by explaining how the page works today and why the work is split into two paths. It also defines each primitive it relies on (queue semantics, multipart upload, bucket lifecycle, signed_url, send_email), and its steps follow the order things actually run. B jumps between paths, so it needs a separate key to say which step belongs where, and it assumes more prior context.

author: sonnet
reason: B is easier to pick up cold: it starts by describing the system as it works today, says why there are two paths (the 60 s request kill, the 900 MB file and the 512 MB worker), and defines every primitive it relies on (queue semantics, multipart upload, bucket rules, signed URLs, the shared row query) before the steps, then closes with a failure table and a verification plan. A covers similar mechanics but assumes more context and scatters its explanations inline.

author: haiku
reason: A starts from today's behaviour and walks through the four stages in order, then sums up the failure cases in a table, so an outsider sees the whole mechanism quickly; B adds depth (a Lua sketch, a replica, rejected alternatives) but cites "requirement N" items it never defines and computes the window key on the gateway clock but Retry-After on Redis's clock, which makes it harder to follow.

author: haiku
reason: B is easier to pick up cold: it opens with what the gateway does today and why limits are being added, then summarises the four stages before going into detail, and its failure table lays out every outcome in one place. A is more thorough, with the actual Lua script and the replica-failover trade-off, but it starts straight in on mechanism and gives a newcomer less to get their bearings.

author: sonnet
reason: A starts from how the system works today and then walks through the request step by step, with each failure handled at the step where it happens, so a newcomer can follow it more easily than B, which opens with a dense diagram and spreads the mechanics across separate notes, even though B is more exact on a few implementation details.

author: sonnet
reason: B is easier for a newcomer: it describes how the gateway works today before adding the change, says why each choice was made (shared Redis, fail open), and walks the request through numbered steps with a failure table, while A has the same mechanics but puts them in a dense diagram and loose notes.

author: haiku
reason: B gives the reason behind each mechanism (why the outbox lives in the database and not the job queue, why pauses use control rows and not flags), defines the switch once as a reusable procedure with a worked pause budget, and uses one consistent set of phase names, while A mixes three stages with four lettered phases and flags its own build-floor inconsistency.

author: haiku
reason: B is the better handover for a newcomer: it first describes how the system works today (primary/replica, version column, flag caching, dead-letter jobs), then explains in plain terms how writes, erases, ids and reads behave, and only then gives the checklist; A is more rigorous and its single reusable procedure S is elegant, but it front-loads dense mechanisms and forward references before you have a picture of the system.

author: sonnet
reason: Document A gives a newcomer one "How the system runs" section that explains writes, repair, copies, deletes, fences, reads and IDs in one place, with scale context up front and a failure-outcome table at the end; Document B spreads the same mechanics across its checklist steps and adds a larger set of flags to track.

author: sonnet
reason: B is easier for a newcomer to understand: it first describes the current system (replica reads, about 38M rows, traffic peaks, the lint rule that keeps all SQL in `UserRepository`), then explains the runtime behaviour in one "How the system runs" section, uses a single write-mode flag where A uses five interacting flags, and ends with a failure table that sums up how the system behaves.

author: haiku
reason: B explains how the system actually works: it has a note on how to read the diagram (rollback boxes are not flag values, and the flag stays put until reconciliation finishes), explicit charge-key rules for safe charging, and the fence, settle and reconcile steps, so a newcomer gets the real mechanism even though B has a small inconsistency about returning to shadow, while A is clean but more surface-level.

author: haiku
reason: A explains why the system works as it does: the charge key doubles as the provider's idempotency key, a note on reading the diagram says the rollback boxes are not flag values and the flag keeps its old value while the fence is up, and it gives the reasons behind the 35-day limit and the "ledger wins" rule, so a newcomer understands the mechanism instead of only following steps; B's failure table and compare-and-set detail are useful, but they don't do this.

author: sonnet
reason: B explains the mechanisms that A leaves vague: how workers learn that charging is paused without a fifth flag value, what the nightly job compares in each mode, how each reconcile outcome is resolved, and the two separate double-charge guards. A is tighter and has the cleaner diagram, but B leaves an outsider with fewer unanswered "but how?" questions.

author: sonnet
reason: A explains the mechanisms an outsider needs and B leaves vague: the four reconcile outcomes for each period, how workers pause charging during a rollback without adding a fifth flag value, and why the idempotency key plus the ledger uniqueness constraint stop double charges even when a worker has a stale flag.

author: haiku
reason: B is the better handover for a newcomer: it opens by naming the four ways checkout can end, then gives a table of what each service stores and the states each record can be in, a failure table that tracks cart, money and stock separately, and a short "why the flow is safe" list tied to labelled diagram steps; A covers about as much ground, but its flowchart is harder to follow and it never states the system's guarantees in one place.

author: haiku
reason: A opens with the four ways checkout can end, defines every term precisely, and adds a per-service stores table, a failure table showing what happens to cart, money and stock, and a list of safety invariants; its diagram also gives every branch an explicit end. B has useful context and a few extra mechanisms, such as the 30-minute provider poll, but its diagram leaves some branches with no end (duplicate webhook, release, stuck refund), and it says the outbox lives only in Payment while Order also publishes events.

author: sonnet
reason: B is slightly better for a newcomer. It explains how to read the diagram, adds a Customer lane that shows what the customer sees, puts each service's tables in its group title, lists the order statuses as a lifecycle, and names where each failure is caught. A's plain-language summary and reasons for the design are strong, but B gives a more complete picture of how the system behaves.

author: sonnet
reason: Document A opens with a one-sentence summary and a guide to reading the diagram, labels every arrow as HTTP or event, defines basic terms like unique constraint and transaction, and gives an explicit order-status tree, so a newcomer could follow the whole system without prior context. B's design rationale and table schemas are useful, but they do not outweigh that.

author: haiku
reason: A starts with a summary of the whole target system and adds a status table, a seven-step walk through one notification and a failure table, so a newcomer gets a working picture fast; B explains the starting point well but never lays out the end-to-end architecture, which leaves the reader to piece it together from the invariants and steps.

author: haiku

reason: A starts with why the change is needed (CPU contention and the cause of the 30 duplicates a week), then describes the running system on its own, with a four-step flow, a state-ownership table and a failure table, before it turns to rollout; B mixes the design into a long, repetitive runbook of 13 steps, so a newcomer has to piece the system together from it.

author: sonnet
reason: B is easier for a newcomer to follow: it states the problem being solved, walks once through the whole runtime flow, uses a table to show who owns each piece of state and another for what happens on each failure, and only then covers the rollout, while A spreads how the system works across thirteen rollout steps.
